newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Chechen decides against controls on journalists.
newsitem.headline: Chechen decides against controls on journalists.

text.p: The Chechen government has decided against a plan to order journalists out of the breakaway Russian region and to allow them only to visit under official protection, Chechnya's interior minister said on Friday.
Kazbek Makhashev said that he had suggested the scheme to evacuate reporters because of concerns for their safety following the latest in a series of kidnappings of journalists.
The government decided against it on Thursday, he said.

Itar-Tass news agency, which employs one of four Russians seized on Tuesday, quoted Deputy Prime Minister Movladi Udugov as saying on Thursday that an order to journalists to leave for their own safety would be issued on Friday.

As well as the four Russians, an Italian photographer is still missing after being seized nearly two weeks ago. Two other Russian journalists were freed last month after several weeks in captivity. Their employer denied it paid a ransom.
The Chechen government has in the past blamed "bandits" seeking ransom for most of the kidnappings.

Interfax news agency quoted an unnamed source on Friday as saying that the Grozny leadership believed the kidnappings were aimed at wrecking negotiations going on with Moscow over a final economic and political settlement to the 21-month Chechen war.

Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin told a news conference in Moscow that negotiations were under way to free this latest set of hostages, but warned that the situation in Chechnya could lead to its isolation.
"My position is far from wanting to isolate the region and republic, but we are moving towards this," he said.
In his annual state of the nation speech on Thursday, President Boris Yeltsin cautioned against rushing peace talks.
"Step by step confidence is being restored. But it is easy to destroy it and for this reason it is dangerous to artificially speed up the negotiating process," Yeltsin said.
His comments contrasted with suggestions by negotiators from both sides last Sunday that a formal peace declaration might be ready for signing soon.
In August the two sides agreed to defer for five years a decision on Chechnya's political status. But Chechnya's separatist leaders still demand full independence and Moscow has ruled this out.
